body.p: In the Office Action, claims 1-15 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 102(a) as being clearly anticipated by Perez et al. (US 11,958,628). Claims 1-15 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 102(b) as being clearly anticipated by Holzner et al. (US 2012/0312926). Applicant respectfully traverses the foregoing rejections.

Notwithstanding the foregoing, solely in an effort to expedite prosecution, Applicant has amended claim 1 to include the features of claim 13. Specifically, claim 1 now specifies that "the electrical cargo conveying devices comprise drive rollers which are configured to orient from a horizontal orientation into an inclined orientation." Claim 1, supra. This is fully supported. Specifically, in addition claim 13, the Specification explains
According to a development, the cargo conveying devices can have drive
rollers, which are designed to orient from a horizontal orientation into an inclined
orientation.
A cargo conveying device may be equipped for this purpose with one or

more suitable actuators, which can adjust one or more drive rollers of the respective cargo conveying device accordingly relative to a horizontal orientation within the cargo hold, so that, for example, a slight angle of inclination relative to a floor of the cargo hold can be set. This can be used, for example, to compensate for an offset or slipping of the cargo items along the cargo compartment floor. By appropriately compensating for unevenly balanced and/or slipping cargo, mechanical stress or even damage and, for example, jamming of the cargo items
can be avoided.
Specification 0034 and 0035; see also Id. 0059. Such features are neither disclosed nor suggested by the cited art.
With respect to the rejections based on Holzner, the Office Action states:
Claim(s) 1-15 is/are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 1021b as being clearly anticipated by Holzmer et al.

Office Action page 2. There is nothing more stated in the Office Action explaining or identify where or how Holzner clearly discloses "drive rollers which are configured to orient from a horizontal orientation into an inclined orientation."

While Applicant does not dispute that Holzner discloses "drive rollers 102a, 102b," Applicant does not believe that Holzner provides any disclosure or suggestion that the provided drive rollers are "configured to orient from a horizontal orientation into an inclined orientation."
Rather, with respect to the drive rollers 102a, 102b, Holzner states:
Rotating plate 103 accommodates a roller drive unit 107 which actuates

drive rollers 102 a, 102 b. Drive rollers 102 a, 102 b are configured to propel freight items in a direction transverse to the rotary axis of drive rollers 102 a, 102 b essentially within the X-Y plane. FIG. 3 shows freight conveying device 100 in an orientation in which it can propel the freight items in the aircraft's transverse direction (X direction). It should be obvious for the person skilled in the art working in this field that the freight items can be propelled in the opposite
direction by actuating drive rollers 102 a, 102 b in an opposing direction. Holzner 0050. Additionally, Holzner explains
Freight conveying devices 100, 110, . . . , 240 described are configured

only to actuate drive rollers 102 a, 102 b when they are activated and if a freight item (e.g. freight container 30) is located directly over them. However, some or all freight conveying devices 100, 110, . . . , 240 may also be configured, in the activated state, to actuate drive rollers 102 a, 100 b regardless of the presence of a
freight item.
Holzner 0060.

Neither of these portions include any teaching or suggestion of a drive roller that is "configured to orient from a horizontal orientation into an inclined orientation." Accordingly, Holzner does not and cannot be said to anticipate claim 1.
Similarly, with respect to Perez, the Office Action merely states
Claim(s) 1-15 is/are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 1021a as being clearly anticipated by Perez et al. 11958628.

Office Action page 2. There is nothing more stated in the Office Action explaining or identify where or how Perez clearly discloses "drive rollers which are configured to orient from a horizontal orientation into an inclined orientation."

Applicant does not dispute that Perez discloses a system that includes "drive rollers 108", again, there is nothing in Perez about the drive rollers 108 being "configured to orient from a horizontal orientation into an inclined orientation."
Specifically, Perez explains that
In various embodiments, one or more of the plurality of trays 104 is

positioned longitudinally along the cargo deck 112-e.g., along the X-direction extending from the forward end to the aft end of the aircraft. In various embodiments, the plurality of conveyance rollers 106 and the one or more drive rollers 108 may be configured to facilitate transport of the ULD 120 in the forward and the aft directions along the conveyance surface 102. Similarly, one or more of the plurality of trays 104 is positioned laterally along the cargo deck 112-e.g., along the Y-direction extending from a starboard side to a port side of the aircraft-and the plurality of conveyance rollers 106 and the one or more drive rollers 108 may be configured to facilitate transport of the ULD 120 in the
starboard and port directions along the conveyance surface 102.
Perez col. 4 lines 53-61.
Perez does explain that
In various embodiments, the one or more drive rollers 108 may be raised

from a lowered position beneath the conveyance surface 102 to an elevated position above the conveyance surface 102 by the corresponding PDU. As used with respect to cargo handling system 100, the term "beneath" may refer to the negative Z-direction, and the term "above" may refer to the positive Z-direction with respect to the conveyance surface 102. In the elevated position, the one or more drive rollers 108 variously contact and drive the ULD 120 that otherwise
rides on the plurality of conveyance rollers 106.

Perez col. 5 lines 8-18. However, an "elevated position above the conveyance surface 102" is not the same as an inclined orientation as that term is used in accordance with the Specification and claims. Moreover, there is nothing inherent about an elevated position being inclined. Indeed, since the rollers in the elevated position "contact and drive the ULD 120," such indicates a raised horizontal orientation in order to contact the ULD 120.
Accordingly, Perez cannot be said to anticipate claim 1 since it fails to disclose a drive roller that is "configured to orient from a horizontal orientation into an inclined orientation."

Therefore, claim 1 includes features that are neither disclosed nor suggested in the cited art. Thus, claim 1 cannot be anticipated by same. Since neither reference discloses a drive roller that is "configured to orient from a horizontal orientation into an inclined orientation," claim 1 cannot be considered obvious since a prima face case of obviousness requires all claim limitations to be taught or suggested by prior art. CFMT, Inc. v. Yieldup Int'l Corp., 68 USPQ2d 1333, 1342 (Fed. Cir. 2003).
In view of the foregoing, claim 1 is allowable over the cited art. Those claims that depend therefrom or refer thereto should be allowable as well.

Applicant therefore respectfully submits that all of the claims of the application should be found to be allowable and thus requests that the Examiner indicate all of the claims as allowed and pass the application to allowance.

The amendments to the claims were done merely to expedite prosecution of the present case. Applicant reserves any and all rights to pursue the subject matter of the original claims in this application, or in another application. Moreover, these amendments should not be construed as an admission or acquiescence to any rejection.

Furthermore, the fact that Applicant has only addressed certain rejections should not be considered to be acquiescence to the rejections. Rather, Applicant has presented the argument herein in an effort to expedite prosecution. Applicant reserves any and all rights to address any rejection made but not specifically addressed herein.
